translation_policy: Original English renderings prepared from the pinned Sanskrit Śrīdhara Svāmī (Bhāvārtha-dīpikā) blocks. They are not substituted with Vedabase purports or copied from an unverified third-party translation; the complete Sanskrit remains the source text.

entries.text: Śrīdhara begins with invocations to Nṛsiṃha, Kṛṣṇa, and his teachers, and declares that he will explain the Bhāgavata according to the received tradition. Vyāsa, having found no satisfaction after composing many scriptures, receives Nārada’s instruction to present the Lord’s qualities and begins this Purāṇa with remembrance of its supreme subject. The word “truth” gives the intrinsic characteristic of the Supreme: the threefold material creation appears real through dependence on Him, although it is not ultimately real in itself. The example of mistaking one element for another illustrates how a dependent appearance is superimposed upon its basis; the Lord’s own radiance removes this deception. “From whom creation, preservation, and dissolution arise” gives the marginal characteristic: He is the intelligent cause of the universe, directly and indirectly present in its effects, yet independent. He is fully conscious, unlike inert primordial nature or the dependent individual soul, and He alone reveals Vedic knowledge to Brahmā. Even the great sages and gods can be bewildered by His power. Śrīdhara also reads the opening “we meditate” as an allusion to the Gāyatrī and presents the Bhāgavata as a revelation of brahma-vidyā.

Śrīdhara explains that this verse establishes the Bhāgavata’s superiority over the three divisions of Vedic scripture. Its supreme dharma rejects every deceptive motive, including the desire for material results and even the separate desire for liberation; it teaches worship of the Lord alone. It is intended for the non-envious and compassionate, and it reveals the real substance rather than merely categories such as substances and qualities. That reality includes the Lord, the individual souls, His māyā, and the universe dependent upon Him. Knowledge of it brings auspiciousness and uproots the three kinds of suffering. Whereas other disciplines may establish the Lord in the heart only after long practice, the Bhāgavata places Him there immediately in those whose desire to hear it arises from spiritual merit.

The Bhāgavata is not merely one more scripture to be heard: Śrīdhara identifies it as the fruit of the Vedic wish-fulfilling tree. Nārada brought it from the higher realm to Vyāsa, Vyāsa placed it in Śuka’s mouth, and from Śuka it descended to the earth through the succession of teacher and disciple. Its sweetness is compared to fruit touched by Śuka, while its essence is the liquid of supreme bliss described by the Upaniṣad. The address to connoisseurs of spiritual rasa invites those capable of tasting that exceptional joy to drink this narration with attention.

Having shown the scripture’s subject, purpose, excellence, and sweetness, Śrīdhara turns to the setting of its narration. Naimiṣa is explained through the wheel made by Brahmā: the place where its rim was broken became the auspicious forest of the sages. Supporting accounts from the Purāṇas are cited to establish the sanctity of the site. The sages therefore gathered there for their sacrificial observance and became prepared to hear the Bhāgavata.

The sages are described as those whose prescribed fire offerings have been properly completed—whether the evening offerings, the morning offerings, or offerings made with the required oblations. Śrīdhara takes this as an indication that their daily and occasional duties were complete, leaving them properly prepared to ask their questions with reverence.

The sages praise Sūta’s authority before questioning him. He has studied the histories, including the Mahābhārata, together with the associated traditions, and he has not merely memorized the Dharmaśāstras but has explained them. His command of the whole field of sacred learning makes him qualified to answer the questions that follow.

Śrīdhara explains that Sūta knows what Vyāsa knew: the Veda and the distinction between the higher and lower Brahman. The sages ask him to speak because he has received the teaching through the mercy of the learned and because love for the hearers makes the teachers reveal even what is hidden. Their request is therefore not for a superficial account but for the truth that leads to understanding.

The sages ask Sūta to speak directly and without difficulty about the highest good—the unfailing means of attaining genuine welfare. Śrīdhara takes “easily” to refer to a straightforward scripture and “highest good” to the good that does not change or fail.

In the age of Kali, people generally live briefly, are lazy, confused, unfortunate, obstructed by troubles, and afflicted by disease. Śrīdhara explains that such people cannot reasonably be expected to master many scriptures through prolonged study. The sages therefore seek a teaching suited to their actual condition.

Even hearing many scriptures is not by itself enough to produce the desired result. Śrīdhara explains that the sages ask Sūta to extract and present the essence—the word whose meaning is properly drawn out and through which the mind and understanding become fully pacified.

The sages begin another question with an auspicious blessing for Sūta, but they keep the blessing concise so that the flow of the Lord’s narrative is not interrupted. Śrīdhara explains “Bhagavān” as the Lord endowed with unsurpassed divine powers, and “Sātvata” as the devotee whose worship is directed toward Him. He is the protector of those devotees, and He appeared in Devakī’s womb in order to accomplish the special purpose for which Vasudeva prayed.

The sages address Sūta affectionately and ask him to narrate the incarnation of the Lord. Śrīdhara explains that the Lord’s descent is, in general, for the protection and welfare of living beings and for their growth in auspiciousness.

The sages reveal why they are eager to hear the Lord’s deeds. Even one overcome by worldly existence is freed from its fear by uttering the Lord’s name; indeed, the name itself is feared by the fear of saṃsāra. Those sages who have taken shelter of the Lord’s feet purify others immediately merely by their presence, whereas the waters of the Gaṅgā—though arising from those feet—purify through continued contact. The Lord’s fame is praised because hearing it removes the impurity of Kali and quiets the suffering of worldly life.
